questions.prompt: One whole ribbon is cut into ten equal pieces. What decimal describes one piece of that whole?
questions.explanation: One piece out of ten is one tenth. The first place after the decimal point counts tenths, so we write 0.1.

questions.prompt: Which decimal is the same amount as 0.5?
questions.explanation: Five tenths fill the same space as fifty hundredths. The final zero in 0.50 does not change that amount.

options: Three whole metres and one tenth
One whole metre and three tenths
questions.explanation: The 1 before the point counts whole metres. The 3 just after it counts tenths of a metre.

sections.title: What are tenths and hundredths?
sections.html:
A tenth is one of ten equal parts of a whole: 1/10 = 0.1. A hundredth is one of 100 equal parts: 1/100 = 0.01. The first digit after the decimal point counts tenths; the second counts hundredths.

Picture a ribbon exactly one metre long. Ten equal pieces give you tenths. Cut each piece into ten again and you have 100 little pieces: hundredths. OpenStax explains the place values.

sections.title: Five tenths as a decimal
sections.html:
Five tenths is 0.5. Five of the ten equal ribbon pieces reach halfway along the original metre. So 5/10, 0.5 and one half describe the same length.

Read 0.5 as �zero point five�. The point separates the whole-number part from the smaller parts; it does not mean �add� or �multiply�.

sections.title: Read one place at a time
sections.html:
Tenths and hundredths in decimals
DecimalMeaning
0.1One tenth
0.01One hundredth
0.25Two tenths and five hundredths: 25 hundredths
1.3One whole and three tenths

In 1.3 metres, the 1 counts complete metres and the 3 counts tenth-metre pieces. The position tells you the size.

sections.title: Why does 0.5 equal 0.50, but not 0.05?
sections.html:
Five tenths and fifty hundredths cover the same amount. Cutting each of your five pieces into ten gives you 50 smaller pieces, without changing their total length. That is why 0.5 = 0.50.

But 0.05 is only five hundredths: five of the tiny pieces, rather than fifty. Moving a digit changes its place value; adding a zero at the end of the decimal here does not.

Continue with fractions that describe the same amount or the friendly guide to basic arithmetic.
